chapters.title: Chapter 1. Mr. Sherlock Holmes
chapters.synopsis: At 221B Baker Street, Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. Watson to deduce the character of a visitor, Dr. James Mortimer, from the walking stick he left behind the night before. Watson reasons that Mortimer is an elderly country doctor given the stick by a hunt, and Holmes corrects him, inferring a young Charing Cross Hospital house-surgeon with a spaniel. Watson checks the Medical Directory, and Holmes sees the dog on the doorstep as Mortimer returns. Mortimer proves to be a tall, stooped, peering man who is fascinated by Holmes's skull, though he is mistaken about the occasion of the gift, which was his marriage. He says he faces a serious and extraordinary problem, and Holmes presses him to state it plainly.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Curse of the Baskervilles
chapters.synopsis: In the Baker Street rooms, Dr. Mortimer produces a 1742 family manuscript entrusted to him by Sir Charles Baskerville and reads it aloud. It tells how the wicked Hugo Baskerville abducted a yeoman's daughter, chased her across the moor with hounds, and was killed by a gigantic black hound, which has supposedly plagued the family since. Mortimer then reads a Devon County Chronicle account of Sir Charles's recent death in the yew alley of Baskerville Hall, ruled natural by the inquest, with heir Henry Baskerville in America. Mortimer finally confides private facts he withheld from the inquest: Sir Charles's obsession with the legend, a black calf-like creature seen weeks earlier, and his own discovery of fresh footprints near the body, which he declares were those of a gigantic hound.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Problem
chapters.synopsis: In the Baker Street sitting room, Dr. Mortimer answers Holmes's questions about the yew alley, the moor-gate, and the footprints, and admits he half-believes the supernatural explanation after learning that three people saw a spectral creature on the moor before Sir Charles died. He explains that Sir Henry Baskerville, the heir who has been farming in Canada, arrives at Waterloo within the hour, and asks what to do with him. Holmes tells him to meet Sir Henry, say nothing, and bring him to Baker Street at ten the next morning. Holmes spends the day smoking and studying an Ordnance map of the moor, and when Watson returns that evening he deduces that Watson spent the day at his club. Holmes then reasons that Sir Charles was running in terror rather than walking on tiptoe, and that he was waiting for someone at the moor-gate the night before he was to leave for London.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Sir Henry Baskerville
chapters.synopsis: At ten o'clock Dr. Mortimer brings Sir Henry Baskerville to Baker Street, where Sir Henry shows Holmes an anonymous letter, made of words pasted from the Times, warning him to keep away from the moor. Holmes deduces the words came from a Times leader, that nail-scissors and gum were used, and that the address was probably written in a hotel. Sir Henry also mentions a newly bought boot that was stolen from outside his hotel door. After hearing Mortimer's story, Sir Henry resolves to go to Baskerville Hall regardless of danger and invites Holmes and Watson to lunch at two. Holmes and Watson follow the two men through Regent Street and spot a bearded man watching them from a hansom cab, but he escapes; Holmes notes the cab number 2704. Holmes then sends the messenger boy Cartwright to search the waste-paper of twenty-three Charing Cross hotels for the mutilated Times page.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Three Broken Threads
chapters.synopsis: After a gallery visit, Holmes and Watson reach the Northumberland Hotel, where Holmes checks the register and finds the people watching Sir Henry are not lodging there. Sir Henry is furious over a second missing boot, an old black one; the missing brown boot is then found under a cabinet in the sitting-room. Holmes questions Mortimer about Barrymore, who has a black beard, and about Sir Charles's will, learning the estate was close on a million, with seven hundred and forty thousand pounds left to Sir Henry and the entail passing to the Desmonds. Holmes cannot leave London because of a blackmail case, so he asks Watson to accompany Sir Henry to Devonshire on Saturday's ten-thirty train from Paddington. Two telegrams show Barrymore is at the Hall and Cartwright could not trace the Times sheet, and cabman John Clayton reveals his fare, a bearded man, gave his name as Sherlock Holmes, which breaks the third thread. Holmes admits he is uneasy about sending Watson.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Baskerville Hall
chapters.synopsis: Holmes sees Watson, Sir Henry and Dr. Mortimer off at the station, instructing Watson to report facts only and to watch the people around Sir Henry, including the Barrymores, Stapleton and his sister, and Frankland. Holmes warns Sir Henry not to go about alone and to avoid the moor in the dark. They travel to Devon, where soldiers are seen hunting Selden, the Notting Hill murderer who has escaped from Princetown. Perkins drives them to Baskerville Hall, where Barrymore receives them and says he and his wife wish to leave. After a gloomy dinner, Watson lies awake at night and hears a woman sobbing somewhere in the house.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. The Stapletons of Merripit House
chapters.synopsis: The morning after arriving, Watson and Sir Henry discuss the sobbing heard in the night; Barrymore denies it was his wife, but Watson sees Mrs. Barrymore's red, swollen eyes and concludes he lied. Watson walks to Grimpen to check the test telegram and learns it was given to Mrs. Barrymore, not Barrymore himself, so the test proves nothing. On the way back he meets the naturalist Stapleton, who shows him the deadly Grimpen Mire, a pony dying in it, an eerie moaning sound on the moor, and prehistoric stone huts. Stapleton's sister Beryl urgently tells Watson to go back to London, mistaking him for Sir Henry, then later retracts it as a whim and attributes it to fear of the family curse. Watson goes to Merripit House, hears Stapleton's background, and returns to the Hall with deepened unease.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. First Report of Dr. Watson
chapters.synopsis: Chapter 8 begins Watson's transcribed letters to Holmes, dated October 13th from Baskerville Hall. Watson describes the moor's prehistoric remains, the apparent flight of the escaped convict, and Sir Henry's growing attraction to Miss Stapleton, which her brother seems to disapprove of. He recounts the excursion to the site of Hugo's legend, Dr. Mortimer's tour of the yew alley, and the litigious neighbour Mr. Frankland with his telescope. Barrymore claims his wife handed him the test telegram, and that night Watson follows him and sees him at an empty room's window staring out at the moor with a candle, then groaning and extinguishing it. Watson and Sir Henry plan a campaign based on this.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Light upon the Moor [Second Report of Dr. Watson]
chapters.synopsis: At Baskerville Hall, Watson writes his second report to Holmes. He examines the window Barrymore used and tells Sir Henry, who agrees to help watch the butler. Sir Henry slips off alone to meet Miss Stapleton on the moor; Watson follows and sees Stapleton run at them in a rage and lead his sister away. Stapleton later apologises and the two agree Sir Henry will court her only as a friend for three months, and the men are to dine at Merripit House on Friday. On the second night's vigil Watson and Sir Henry catch Barrymore signalling with a candle. Mrs. Barrymore reveals she is Selden's sister and that they are feeding him on the moor. The men chase Selden by the signal candle near the Cleft Tor after hearing the hound-like cry, and Watson glimpses a tall, thin, unknown man standing on a tor.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Extract from the Diary of Dr. Watson
chapters.synopsis: On 16 October, the morning after the chase on the moor, Watson reflects on the hound and the stranger on the tor, and resolves to find the man himself. Barrymore protests the hunting of Selden, pledges that the convict will soon sail for South America, and Sir Henry agrees not to tell the police. Barrymore then reveals that Sir Charles received a letter from Coombe Tracey signed L. L. asking him to be at the gate at ten, and that his wife found its charred remains. On 17 October Watson walks the rainy moor to the tor, and Dr. Mortimer, who tells him of Laura Lyons, Frankland's estranged daughter in Coombe Tracey, whose initials are L. L. That evening Barrymore tells Watson that Selden knows of another hidden man on the moor, a gentleman-like stranger living in the stone huts and fed by a lad, and Watson resolves to reach the heart of the mystery.

chapters.title: Chapter 11. The Man on the Tor
chapters.synopsis: Watson drives to Coombe Tracey and questions Mrs. Laura Lyons, who admits she wrote the letter asking Sir Charles to meet her at the gate at ten but swears she never went, citing a private matter and a divorce-related need for money. Watson finds her story coherent but feels something is held back. On the way back he meets Mr. Frankland, who gloats over legal victories and reveals that he has seen, through his telescope, a boy carrying food to a hidden person on the moor. Watson follows the boy's path to a circle of stone huts near Black Tor and finds a hut that is clearly inhabited, with a note reading 'Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.' Waiting in the dusk with his revolver cocked, he hears footsteps and is greeted by a well-known voice.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. Death on the Moor
chapters.synopsis: Inside the stone hut near Black Tor, Watson finds that the hidden stranger is Sherlock Holmes, who has secretly lodged on the moor with the boy Cartwright and has read all of Watson's reports. Holmes reveals that Stapleton is a former schoolmaster whose supposed sister Beryl is actually his wife, and that he is plotting murder. A terrible scream and the rumble of a hound draw them across the moor, where they find a body in Sir Henry's ruddy tweed suit. It proves to be the convict Selden, wearing Sir Henry's old clothes passed on by Barrymore. Stapleton then arrives, visibly shaken to find the wrong man dead, and Holmes feigns that he is returning to London while privately explaining that they lack proof. Holmes and Watson walk to Baskerville Hall, with Holmes ordering Watson to say nothing of the hound to Sir Henry.

chapters.title: Chapter 13. Fixing the Nets
chapters.synopsis: At Baskerville Hall Holmes joins Sir Henry and Watson, explains little, and asks Sir Henry to obey blindly. Studying the family portraits, Holmes spots that the portrait of the wicked Hugo bears a striking resemblance to Stapleton, concluding Stapleton is a Baskerville with designs on the succession. Next morning Holmes arranges a ruse: he and Watson will feign leaving for London while Sir Henry walks home alone across the moor from Merripit House after dining with the Stapletons. At Coombe Tracey station Holmes wires Lestrade, who is coming with an unsigned warrant, and visits Laura Lyons. He shows her proof that Stapleton is married to Beryl, and she, furious, confesses that Stapleton dictated the letter to Sir Charles and then dissuaded her from the appointment and made her keep silent. Holmes meets Lestrade at the station and promises him a night on Dartmoor.

chapters.title: Chapter 14. The Hound of the Baskervilles
chapters.synopsis: Holmes, Watson and Lestrade return to the moor at night and hide near Merripit House, where Watson sees Stapleton leave the dining-room and briefly visit an out-house while Sir Henry dines. A fog rolls in from Grimpen Mire, but Sir Henry emerges walking home and is pursued by a huge phosphorus-daubed black hound, which Holmes and Watson shoot dead after it knocks Sir Henry down. Searching Merripit House, they find Beryl Stapleton bound and whipped in the museum room, and she tells them Stapleton's refuge is an old tin mine on an island in the mire. Stapleton is never found; next morning they follow her marked path into the mire, recover Sir Henry's missing boot, and conclude that Stapleton drowned in the bog. On the island they find the hound's kennel, a dead spaniel skeleton and the luminous paste, and Holmes explains how the device was used to terrify Sir Charles and Selden.

chapters.title: Chapter 15. A Retrospection
chapters.synopsis: At the end of November in Baker Street, Holmes, now free from two other cases, recounts the whole Baskerville affair to Watson. He explains that Stapleton was Rodger Baskerville's son, who fled to England as Vandeleur, ran a failing school in Yorkshire, then moved to Devon to claim the estate. Holmes details how the phosphorus-daubed hound killed Sir Charles, how Laura Lyons and Beryl were used and manipulated, and how the boot, warning letter and London shadowing fit together. He explains his own secret stay on the moor with Cartwright, and the bait plan that ended in Stapleton's destruction. Sir Henry and Mortimer are about to take a long voyage, and Holmes closes by inviting Watson to the opera and dinner.

summary.text: Sherlock Holmes, addressed as Mr. Holmes, is the investigator whom Dr. Mortimer and Sir Henry consult, and he is shown as a methodical reasoner who insists that all other hypotheses be exhausted before the supernatural one is accepted, and who can deduce a man's habits from the gloss on his hat and boots. Early on he tells Watson to report facts fully and leave the theorizing to him, and he begs Sir Henry not to go about alone. Watson, who supposes that a blackmail case is absorbing all of Holmes's faculties, comes to believe that a tall, thin figure on the tor and a hidden stranger in the old stone huts, served by a lad who brings supplies, are someone else; in fact, as the narrator states in chapter 12, that hidden stranger is Holmes himself. Holmes explains that he remained an unknown factor ready to throw in all his weight at a critical moment, that he had read Watson's well-thumbed reports, and that he stayed mostly at Coombe Tracey, using the hut only when he needed to be near the scene of action. He admits his own bungled pursuit once betrayed him to a shadow, and he tells Watson that against Stapleton they have only surmise and no provable case, so he plans to make Stapleton believe that he and Watson have gone to London while they secretly return.

summaries.text: Sherlock Holmes is a reasoner who appears in the opening chapters in conversation with Watson and in consultation with Mortimer. In chapter 1 he tells Watson that most of his conclusions were erroneous, and in chapter 2 he states that he had recently been preoccupied with the Vatican cameos affair for the Pope. In chapter 3 he instructs Mortimer to say nothing to Sir Henry until he has made up his mind, and asks Mortimer to call at ten o'clock the next day bringing Sir Henry. He also insists that all other hypotheses be exhausted before falling back on the supernatural one, and he deduces from a man's returning immaculate in the evening, with gloss on hat and boots, that the man has been a fixture all day.

appearance.text: Sherlock Holmes is a tall, austere figure (ch 6). Seen at the door of a hut, he cut a dark, athletic outline, with his shoulders stooping and his head thrust forward (ch 12).

personality.text: Holmes is a rationalist who insists that all other hypotheses be exhausted before a more extraordinary one is accepted (ch 3). He is secretive about his thinking, telling a companion to say nothing to another man until he has made up his mind (ch 3), and he is controlling in his methods, asking Watson to report facts in full and leave the theorizing to him (ch 6). He is nonetheless candid about his own errors, admitting that he and Watson have betrayed themselves and lost their man (ch 4). His frankness and directness in interviews can considerably amaze those he questions (ch 13). Beneath this he is protective and caring, begging Sir Henry not to go about alone (ch 6) and breathing a prayer of gratitude on seeing that there was no sign of a wound (ch 14).

history.arc: The Baskerville Legend and Sir Henry's Arrival
history.text: Holmes was the friend and companion of Dr. Watson, who chronicled his cases and wrote accounts of his achievements to give publicity to his methods (ch1). When Dr. Mortimer consulted him about a serious and extraordinary problem, Holmes told Watson that most of his conclusions were erroneous (ch1). He had recently been preoccupied with the Vatican cameos affair for the Pope when Mortimer consulted him about the death of Sir Charles Baskerville (ch2). He insisted that all other hypotheses be exhausted before falling back on the supernatural one, told Mortimer to say nothing to Sir Henry until he had made up his mind, asked him to call at ten o'clock the next day with Sir Henry, and asked Watson to help (ch3). From his Baker Street rooms, Holmes, who claimed to identify newspaper types at a glance as a special expert in crime, employed Cartwright to search hotel waste-paper for the Times page. He accepted an invitation to lunch from Henry Baskerville at the Northumberland Hotel at two, and admitted that his own bungled pursuit had betrayed him to the shadow (ch4). Holmes said that one of the most revered names in England was being besmirched by a blackmailer and that only he could stop a disastrous scandal, and he suspected that Barrymore might be the black-bearded man following Sir Henry (ch5).

Holmes was revealed as the hidden stranger on the moor, his voice recognized as his own (ch12), and he occupied the stone hut as his hideout while Cartwright, whom he employed, brought down his supplies (ch12). He remained an unknown factor in the business, ready to throw in all his weight at a critical moment, and he received Watson's well-thumbed reports (ch12), which he called incriminating (ch13). Holmes, a friend of Watson and the enemy of Stapleton, told Stapleton he would take an unpleasant remembrance back to London with him the next day, though he admitted they lacked a provable case against him, only surmise (ch12). He planned to make Stapleton believe he and Watson had gone to London, using Sir Henry as the channel, while they secretly returned (ch13), and he sent Cartwright on errands to London and the station office, corresponded with his colleague Lestrade, and sent a report to Princetown from Grimpen about the death of Selden (ch13). Allied with Lestrade in the ambush at Merripit House, Holmes killed the Hound of the Baskervilles (ch14), and he later recalled being conscious of a faint smell of white jessamine and explained that he had stayed mostly at Coombe Tracey, using the hut on the moor only when he needed to be near the scene of action (ch15).

personality.text: Dr. Watson is an observant and analytical man, able to reason from small clues to a considered judgment, as when he judges it probable that a visitor is a country practitioner who does much of his visiting on foot (ch 1). He is also obliging, readily agreeing to join in an undertaking with the words "I will come, with pleasure" (ch 5). He is candid about his limitations, admitting that although he tried one or two explanations, he "was completely puzzled myself" (ch 9). Yet he is easily alarmed by the unknown, saying his blood ran cold when he heard a break in another man's voice that told of sudden horror (ch 9).

history.text: In chapter 6 Sherlock Holmes asked Dr. Watson to report the facts of the case from Devonshire, advised him to keep his revolver near him night and day and never relax his precautions, and Watson heard the muffled, strangling sob of a woman torn by uncontrollable sorrow (ch 6). In chapter 7 he was a friend of Henry Baskerville and of Holmes, and of Dr. James Mortimer, a mutual friend with Mr. Stapleton, who was acquainted with him (ch 7). He wrote to Holmes about events at Baskerville Hall (ch 8), stayed there, and hunted Selden on the moor with Sir Henry (ch 9). As Holmes's agent he sent written reports from the Hall and received short notes from Baker Street, learned from Barrymore about the other man on the moor, and resolved to play his own game and speak as little as possible to anyone (ch 10). In chapter 11 a well-known voice greeted him as 'my dear Watson' and said he would be more comfortable outside than in, and it emerged that Sir Henry had at first been eager to come but that they had agreed the results might be better if Watson went alone (ch 11).

summary.text: Dr. James Mortimer, who insists on being called "Mister" as a humble M.R.C.S., is a very tall, thin man with a long beak-like nose, keen grey eyes set closely together, and gold-rimmed glasses. Dr. Watson states that he was house-surgeon at Charing Cross Hospital from 1882 to 1884 and is now Medical Officer for the parishes of Grimpen, Thorsley, and High Barrow; he is also a trustee and executor of Sir Charles's will, from which he himself received a thousand pounds. He comes to Sherlock Holmes with what he calls a serious and extraordinary problem, and admits he covets Holmes's skull, though Holmes says he called for a further purpose. Mortimer says he withheld information from the inquest because a man of science shrinks from seeming to endorse a popular superstition, and he claims to have found hound footprints near the body that he told no one about, though he says he does not know what to believe. Holmes, by deduction, believes him to be a young, amiable, unambitious, absent-minded man with a favourite dog, and Mortimer is later much troubled over the disappearance of his little spaniel, which Holmes believes he will never see again.

He says his stick was given to him by friends at the hospital on the occasion of his marriage, and that he covets Holmes's skull. Holmes, by deduction, believes Mortimer to be a young fellow under thirty, amiable, unambitious, absent-minded, and the owner of a favourite dog. Holmes states that Mortimer called on him the previous night and again that day for a purpose beyond examining the skull, and Mortimer says he has come because he faces a serious and extraordinary problem.

Mortimer insisted he was a humble "Mister", said he coveted Holmes's skull, and came to consult Holmes about a serious and extraordinary problem (ch1). He was the medical attendant and friend of Sir Charles Baskerville, who had entrusted the manuscript to him, and he had withheld information from the inquest because a man of science shrinks from seeming to endorse a popular superstition (ch2). He believed the fresh footprints he found away from the body were of a gigantic hound, and he had glimpsed something he took to be a large black calf (ch2). He admitted he had said nothing about the prints, could not call Holmes in earlier without disclosing the facts to the world, and did not know what to believe (ch3). As trustee and executor of Sir Charles's will (ch3), he arranged to meet Sir Henry at Waterloo Station, and he had been staying with a friend rather than at the Northumberland Hotel (ch4); he himself received a thousand pounds from the will (ch5).

summary.text: Sir Charles Baskerville was a childless widower who made his fortune in South African speculation and returned to England to settle at Baskerville Hall, where he lived for two years before his death. He entrusted the family manuscript to Dr. James Mortimer, his friend and medical attendant, who stated that Sir Charles avoided the moor at night and once asked whether Mortimer had ever seen a strange creature or heard a hound baying on his night journeys. On the fourth of May, Sir Charles announced he would leave for London the next day, and his body was found at the far end of the alley; the coroner's jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence. Mortimer stated that cigar ash showed Sir Charles had stood at the moor-gate for five or ten minutes before dying, and Barrymore stated that his footprints changed character after the gate, as if he walked on his toes. Sherlock Holmes initially believed Sir Charles was running desperately for his life, crazed with fear, and had waited at the gate the night before his departure, and later stated that he died of heart disease and terror while fleeing the hound down the yew alley.

history.arc: The Baskerville Legend and Sir Henry's Arrival
history.text: Sir Charles Baskerville, a descendant of Hugo Baskerville (ch 2), made his fortune in South African speculation and returned to England to settle at Baskerville Hall, where he lived for about two years (ch 2). He was a childless widower (ch 2) whose younger brother was Rodger Baskerville (ch 3), and whose nephew Henry was his next of kin and heir (ch 2). He believed in the curse of the Hound of the Baskervilles (ch 2), entrusted the family manuscript to Dr. James Mortimer, his friend and medical attendant (ch 2), and would not go out onto the moor at night, asking Mortimer whether he had ever seen any strange creature or heard the baying of a hound (ch 2). On the fourth of May he declared his intention of starting next day for London, and his body was then discovered at the far end of the alley (ch 2); Barrymore, his butler, reported that his footprints changed character after the moor-gate, as if he walked on his toes (ch 2), and the coroner's jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence (ch 2). Mortimer stated that he had stood at the moor-gate for five or ten minutes before dying, as shown by cigar ash dropped twice (ch 3), while Holmes believed he had been running desperately for his life, crazed with fear before he began to run, and that he had waited there on the night before his departure (ch 3). His will named Mortimer as executor and trustee (ch 3), left legacies to Barrymore and Mortimer, and made Henry the residuary legatee (ch 5).

summary.text: The Hound of the Baskervilles is the creature at the center of the deaths that have afflicted the Baskerville family, many of whom, the narrator says, met sudden, bloody, and mysterious ends. Dr. James Mortimer reports that three people saw a luminous, ghastly, spectral, huge creature on the moor, and that none has been reported seeing it since; on the moor a deep, muttered rumble, musical yet menacing, is also heard. It later proves to be a real animal rather than a spectre: a cross of bloodhound and mastiff as large as a small lioness, whose flaming look came from a phosphorus preparation that had no smell to hinder its scent, and it is killed by Holmes's revolver shots. Holmes states that Stapleton bought it in London from Ross and Mangles, the dealers in Fulham Road, and kennelled it, and Holmes theorizes, as a belief rather than established fact, that it was set on Selden from an article of Sir Henry's, probably the boot stolen at the hotel.

summary.text: Henry Baskerville, known as Sir Henry Baskerville or Sir Henry, is the heir to the Baskerville estate, the son of Sir Charles's younger brother and, according to Dr. James Mortimer, the last of the Baskervilles. He is about thirty, small, alert and sturdily built, with dark eyes, thick black eyebrows and a strong pugnacious face. He has spent nearly all his time in the States and Canada, where he had been farming, and he arrives in England at Southampton; his father lived in a cottage on the South Coast, and Henry, a boy in his teens when his father died, had never seen the Hall. He has known the family hound story since the nursery but never took it seriously, and he declares that no man on earth can prevent him from going to the home of his own people, even after he receives an anonymous letter at the Northumberland Hotel and one of his boots goes missing. Once at the estate he becomes deeply infatuated with Miss Stapleton, a feeling Dr. Watson believes is mutual, and he later swears from his experience with dogs out West that the hound heard on the moor is real.

history.text: Henry Baskerville was introduced as Sir Charles's next of kin and heir, the son of Sir Charles's younger brother (ch 2), and Dr. Mortimer described him as the nephew of Rodger Baskerville, the last of the Baskervilles, who had been farming in Canada and had wired that he arrived at Southampton that morning (ch 3). When Sir Henry appeared at the Northumberland Hotel, he was about thirty, small, alert, dark-eyed and sturdily built, with thick black eyebrows and a strong pugnacious face, and he said he had spent nearly all his time in the States and Canada (ch 4). He said he had known the hound story since the nursery as the family's pet story but had never taken it seriously, and he declared that no man on earth could prevent him from going to the home of his own people (ch 4). He reported that he had received an anonymous letter, posted at Charing Cross and addressed in rough printed characters, and that one of his boots, put outside his door the night before, was missing in the morning (ch 4). As residuary legatee of Sir Charles, with James Desmond as the heir after him to the entailed estate, he planned to go at the end of the week, feeling that the money should go with the title and estate, and Dr. Watson was to accompany and protect him at Baskerville Hall (ch 5).

Sir Henry became master of Baskerville Hall (ch6), though his father had lived in a little cottage on the South Coast and Henry, a boy in his teens at his father's death, had never seen the Hall (ch6); after that death he lived in America with a friend (ch6). He planned to install electric lights on the avenue within six months (ch6), and he employed Barrymore as butler (ch7), while Dr. Watson, Mr. Stapleton and Dr. James Mortimer were counted as his friends (ch7, ch10). Watson believed Sir Henry was strongly attracted to Miss Stapleton from their first meeting and thought the feeling mutual (ch8), and the narrator stated that he was greatly infatuated with her (ch9), although her brother Mr. Stapleton opposed the courtship (ch8, ch9). Sir Henry dismissed the figure on the tor as a warder, a view that was his belief (ch9), and he hunted Selden (ch9) until he agreed not to give Selden up to the police, admitting that they were aiding a felony (ch10).

history.text: Barrymore, the butler at Baskerville Hall and husband of Mrs. Barrymore (ch 6), was kept by Sherlock Holmes on the list of suspects (ch 6), and he told them that he and his wife had been very much attached to Sir Charles, whose death gave them a shock and made their surroundings very painful to them (ch 6); he had discovered Sir Charles's body (ch 7). He told Sir Henry that the sobbing could not have come from his wife (ch 7), and Watson wondered whether he was the bearded man in the Regent Street cab (ch 7, belief). Barrymore said he was in the box-room when his wife brought him the telegram and that he told her what to answer (ch 8), but Watson saw him crouching at the window of an unoccupied room with a candle held against the glass, and he gave a deep groan and impatiently put out the light (ch 8). Mrs. Barrymore explained that he was signalling to Selden that food was ready, and that Selden's light on the moor showed where to bring it (ch 9); the narrator noted that Barrymore was rather deaf and entirely preoccupied (ch 9). It emerged that Barrymore was Selden's brother-in-law, that he was hiding and feeding him on the moor, and that he was the informant who told Watson about the other man there; he said Selden would soon be on his way to South America (ch 10).

summary.text: Jack Stapleton, also known as Vandeleur, is a butterfly-collecting naturalist who carries a net and specimen box and lives at Merripit House on the moor, where he presents himself as living with his sister. He is described as about forty, of middle height, with a square-cut black beard and pale face, and the bearded man in cab No. 2704 whom Holmes calls 'our man' fits this description; Holmes and Watson come to believe he is the spy who dogged them in London. Holmes states that Stapleton is the son of Rodger Baskerville, Sir Charles's younger brother, that he fled to England under the name Vandeleur after taking public money and ran a school in Yorkshire that came to grief, and that the woman posed as his sister is in fact his wife, kept in that role because she would be more useful to him as a free woman. He is also a recognized authority on entomology, and the name Vandeleur is attached to a certain moth. Holmes declares that he is plotting murder, and Watson believes he has designs on the Baskerville succession; Laura Lyons states that he dictated the letter to Sir Charles and frightened her into silence. The narrative implies that he ends up buried in the heart of Grimpen Mire.

summaries.text: Jack Stapleton, also called Mr. Stapleton or simply Stapleton, is a man who carries a butterfly net and a botanical specimen box and lives at Merripit House. He tells Watson that he knew who Watson was because the records of Holmes had reached them on the moor. He also says that Sir Charles's nerves were so worked up that the appearance of any dog might have had a fatal effect on his diseased heart, which is his opinion rather than established fact. Watson observes that Stapleton's greeting to his sister did not seem altogether cordial. Separately, John Clayton describes a spy as about forty, of middle height, with a square-cut black beard and a pale face, and Holmes believes this spy knew his address, knew Sir Henry had consulted him, and recognised him in Regent Street. The material read so far does not say that this spy is Stapleton.

Jack Stapleton, also known as Mr. Stapleton and, under an earlier identity, Vandeleur, is a butterfly-collecting naturalist who lives at Merripit House on the moor, where he says he has been for two years. Holmes states that he is a recognized authority on entomology, that he is the son of Rodger Baskerville (younger brother of Sir Charles), and that after taking a considerable sum of public money he fled to England as Vandeleur and ran a school in the east of Yorkshire, which came to grief under atrocious circumstances. Holmes also states that Stapleton passed off his wife as his sister because she would be more useful to him as a free woman, and that Stapleton is plotting murder; Laura Lyons says he dictated the letter to Sir Charles and frightened her into silence. Watson observes that he disapproves of Sir Henry's attentions to the woman presented as his sister and tries to keep them apart, and Watson believes he has designs on the Baskerville succession. The narrator implies that Stapleton ends up buried in Grimpen Mire, which sucked him in, while Holmes's suspicion that he was the spy who dogged them in London (a belief rather than an established fact at ch12, where Watson asks it as a question) matches the description in ch5 of a man of about forty, of middle height, with a square-cut black beard and a pale face.

personality.text: Jack Stapleton is observant and well-informed, having known Holmes's address, Sir Henry's consultation, and Holmes's identity on sight in Regent Street (ch 5). He is possessive of his sister, taking pains to keep her from being alone with Sir Henry (ch 8), and domineering toward her, beckoning her away in a peremptory way (ch 9). He shows remarkable self-control, mastering his amazement and disappointment through a supreme effort when his plans are upset (ch 12), and Holmes describes his crimes as refined, cold-blooded, deliberate murder (ch 12). He is also manipulative, frightening a woman into silence by warning that she would be suspected if the facts came out (ch 13), and brutal, as shown by the red weal of a whiplash across her neck (ch 14).

history.text: Holmes listed Mr. Stapleton among the people to be studied (ch 6). Stapleton, who carried a butterfly net and botanical specimen box and lived at Merripit House, was a friend of Dr. Mortimer and of Henry Baskerville, and he knew Watson's identity because the records of Holmes had reached them on the moor (ch 7). He said he had been on the moor two years, and that an epidemic had broken out in a school in which three boys died (ch 7); he also suggested that Sir Charles's nerves were so worked up that the appearance of any dog might have had a fatal effect upon his diseased heart (ch 7, belief). Watson thought his greeting to his sister did not seem altogether cordial (ch 7). Stapleton disapproved when Sir Henry paid attention to his sister, took pains to prevent them being alone together, and exercised a marked influence over her (ch 8). He would not hear of Perkins the groom going over to sleep at Merripit House (ch 8), and Watson believed he shared the popular view of an evil influence on families (ch 8, belief). When Sir Henry persisted, Stapleton turned on his heel and peremptorily beckoned his sister, who walked off by his side after an irresolute glance at Sir Henry (ch 9). The later chapters showed his past kindness: he had financially helped Laura Lyons to earn an honest living (ch 10), and he had been Sir Charles's almoner on several occasions, having told Sir Charles about her affairs after helping her (ch 11).

Holmes declared that Stapleton was plotting murder, and said he had posed his wife as his sister because she would be more useful to him as a free woman (ch12). Holmes had also found that a school had come to grief under atrocious circumstances and that its owner, under a different name, had disappeared with his wife (ch12); Watson, in a question, believed Stapleton was the enemy who had dogged them in London (ch12), and Stapleton turned a ghastly face to them after overcoming his amazement and disappointment by a supreme effort (ch12). Holmes saw Stapleton's face in Hugo's portrait and concluded he was a Baskerville (ch13), and showed that he and his wife had been photographed in York four years earlier, the photograph endorsed 'Mr. and Mrs. Vandeleur' (ch13); Watson believed he had designs on the Baskerville succession (ch13), while Laura Lyons said he had dictated the letter to Sir Charles, telling her it would get help for her divorce costs, and had frightened her into silence by saying she would be suspected if the facts came out (ch13). He could keep the hound in the out-house at Merripit in an emergency, though it was always a risk (ch14), and he was implied to be buried in the heart of Grimpen Mire, which sucked him in (ch14). Holmes revealed that Stapleton was the son of Rodger Baskerville, the younger brother of Sir Charles, and that after purloining a considerable sum of public money he changed his name to Vandeleur, fled to England and established a school in the east of Yorkshire (ch15); he was also a recognized authority on entomology, and the name Vandeleur was permanently attached to a certain moth (ch15).

His fixation extends beyond the courtroom, as he lies on the roof of his house with an excellent telescope and sweeps the moor all day hoping to glimpse the escaped convict (ch 8). history.text: In chapter 6, Sherlock Holmes suspected Mr. Frankland, a resident of Lafter Hall, as an unknown factor (ch 6). In chapter 8, Frankland was shown to have a passion for British law and to have spent a large fortune in litigation, and he swept the moor with a telescope from his roof hoping to spot the convict, while he was rumoured to intend prosecuting Mortimer for digging up the skull (ch 8). In chapter 10, it emerged that Laura Lyons was his daughter, and that he was estranged from her and allowed her only a pittance since she married without his consent (ch 10). In chapter 11, he boasted of having established a right of way through the centre of old Middleton's park, and he believed that the person he saw every day through his rooftop telescope, passing along the same path at the same hour, was going to the convict; he refused to help the police and bound Watson to secrecy about the boy (ch 11). summary.text: Selden, also called the Notting Hill murderer, is a convict whose death sentence was commuted over doubts about his sanity, and who escaped from Princetown, after which the warders were reported to be watching every road and station. Although Dr. Watson notes that, a fortnight after the flight, locals believe he has left the moor, he is in fact still nearby: the Barrymores took him in, and every second night, if he answered a light in the window, Barrymore took bread and meat out to him. Barrymore also passed on Sir Henry's old clothes (boots, shirt, cap) to aid his escape. In a confrontation on the moor, Selden screamed a curse and hurled a rock that splintered against the boulder sheltering those who were with him. Holmes later sent a report from Grimpen to Princetown about Selden's death, and Holmes believes, though it is not confirmed, that Selden ran and screamed because he saw the luminous hound bounding after him in the dark.

Dr. Watson and Sir Henry hunted him there, and he screamed a curse at them and hurled a rock that splintered against the boulder that had sheltered them (ch9). summary.text: Beryl Stapleton, also called Miss Stapleton or Beryl, is a woman who speaks in a low, eager voice with a curious lisp. She is introduced as Stapleton's sister, but Holmes states in chapter 12 that she is in reality his wife, and in chapter 15 he identifies her as Beryl Garcia, one of the beauties of Costa Rica, whom Stapleton married. In chapter 7 she urgently tells Watson to leave for London and never return to the moor, saying she believes in the hound story and fears for Sir Henry, and she hushes when her brother approaches; Watson later observes (ch8) that she glances at him as if seeking approval, which he takes to show the man's marked influence over her. By chapter 14 she bears the red weal of a whiplash across her neck and says she has been Stapleton's dupe and tool, having helped plant the guiding wands that mark the path through the mire and led Holmes to the start of it. According to Holmes (ch15), she tried to warn Sir Henry by sending a letter made from cut-out words in a disguised hand, and Stapleton tied her up so she could not warn him further.

history.text: Beryl Stapleton lived at Merripit House and was a friend of Sir Charles Baskerville (ch 7). She spoke in a low, eager voice with a curious lisp, and she urgently told Watson to leave for London and never return to the moor, then fell silent when her brother approached (ch 7). She said her brother would be very angry if he knew she had said anything which might induce Sir Henry to go away, and she said she believed in the hound story and urged that Sir Henry be taken from a place that had always been fatal to his family (ch 7). Sir Henry was romantically attracted to her, and her brother Mr. Stapleton had a marked influence over her, which Watson saw when she glanced at him as she talked, as if seeking his approval (ch 8). She later told Sir Henry that the moor was dangerous and that she would not be happy until he had left it (ch 9).

In chapter 12 Sherlock Holmes stated that the woman passed off as Miss Stapleton was in reality Stapleton's wife, and she was secretly his wife (ch12, ch13). In chapter 14 she bore the red weal of a whiplash across her neck and said she had been Stapleton's dupe and tool, and she helped plant the guiding wands marking the path through the mire and led Holmes to the start of it (ch14). Chapter 15 revealed her past through Holmes, who said Stapleton had married Beryl Garcia, one of the beauties of Costa Rica (ch15). It also revealed that Henry Baskerville loved her (ch15), and that she warned him by an anonymous cut-out letter, cutting out the words which would form the message and addressing the letter in a disguised hand (ch15). Holmes said Stapleton then tied her up and imprisoned her in her room at the Mexborough Private Hotel so that she might have no chance of warning Sir Henry (ch15).

summary.text: Mrs. Laura Lyons, also known as L. L., is a typewriting businesswoman at Coombe Tracey who, according to Dr. James Mortimer, married an artist named Lyons who came sketching on the moor, proved a blackguard and deserted her; her father, Frankland, refused to have anything to do with her after she married without his consent. Barrymore reports that a burned letter fragment asking its recipient to burn it and be at the gate by ten o'clock, signed with the initials L. L., was connected to Sir Charles, and Mrs. Lyons admits she wrote the letter but swears she never went to the meeting, saying something intervened. She claims she wanted Sir Charles's help to meet expenses tied to freedom from her husband, that she got help elsewhere, and that she learned of his death from the paper next morning; these are her own account, and Watson feels she is holding something back. Holmes states that she and Stapleton meet, write and have a complete understanding, and she says Stapleton offered her marriage on condition that she obtain a divorce. Holmes further states that Stapleton pressed her to write imploring Sir Charles for an interview on the evening before his departure for London, then by a specious argument prevented her from going.

summaries.text: Mrs. Laura Lyons, who also appears under the initials L. L., is introduced in chapter 10 through the account of Dr. James Mortimer, who states that she married an artist named Lyons who came sketching on the moor and that he proved a blackguard and deserted her. Mortimer adds that her father, Frankland, refused to have anything to do with her after she married without his consent, and that Stapleton, Sir Charles and Mortimer himself (who gave a trifle) helped set her up in a typewriting business. In the same chapter Barrymore states that Sir Charles received a letter from Coombe Tracey addressed in a woman's hand, and that a burned fragment of a letter asked the recipient to burn it and be at the gate by ten o'clock, signed with the initials L. L.; the slip crumbled to bits after it was moved. The text as presented here does not itself establish, beyond the matching initials, that Laura Lyons wrote that letter, so any link between her and the burned note remains an inference rather than a stated fact.

Beneath that reserve she is highly emotional, and when pressed she cries out that she did write the letter, "pouring out her soul in a torrent of words" (ch11). Once she has been confronted, she becomes cooperative and openly offers to answer questions, promising that "there is nothing which I shall hold back" (ch13).

history.text: In chapter 10, Barrymore stated that Sir Charles had received a letter from Coombe Tracey addressed in a woman's hand, and that a burned fragment of it asked the recipient to burn the letter and be at the gate by ten o'clock, signed with the initials L. L. (ch 10). Dr. James Mortimer revealed that Laura Lyons, who lived in Coombe Tracey, was the daughter of Mr. Frankland, and that she had married an artist named Lyons who came sketching on the moor, proved a blackguard and deserted her (ch 10). Frankland refused to have anything to do with her after she married without his consent, and Stapleton, Sir Charles and Mortimer, who gave a trifle, helped set her up in a typewriting business (ch 10). In chapter 11 Mrs. Lyons admitted she wrote the letter and swore she never went to the meeting, saying something intervened to prevent her going (ch 11). By her own account, which is her belief and claim, she wanted Sir Charles's help because a chance of freedom from her husband depended on meeting certain expenses, she received help from another source in the interval, and she learned of his death from the paper next morning (ch 11). She also named Stapleton as one of the gentlemen who helped her, through whom Sir Charles learned of her affairs, and she was estranged from her father, to whom she owed nothing, while Watson felt that something was being held back from him by the lady (ch 11).

questions.question: What is the serious and extraordinary problem for which Mortimer seeks Holmes's help?
questions.quote: I am suddenly confronted with a most serious and extraordinary problem.

resolved.answer: Mortimer consults Holmes about the death of Sir Charles Baskerville and the hound legend, supported by fresh giant hound footprints.
resolved.quote: “Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!”
resolved.payoff: In chapter 1 Mortimer says he is 'suddenly confronted with a most serious and extraordinary problem' but withholds its nature, and Holmes presses him to state it plainly. The resolution supplies it: the death of Sir Charles Baskerville tied to the family's hound legend, made extraordinary by Mortimer's revelation that he saw the footprints of a gigantic hound near the body. This fits the setup's 'suddenly confronted' framing, since the footprint discovery is the startling new element that turns an apparent natural death into a puzzle he cannot handle as an 'unpractical man'.

questions.question: Did a real hound kill Sir Charles, and what caused his terror and the toe-walking footprints?
questions.quote: Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!

resolved.answer: Sir Charles was frightened to death by a hound daubed with phosphorus, set on by Stapleton.
resolved.quote: It was suggested, of course, by the story of the family hell-hound, and by the desire to frighten old Sir Charles to death.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 2 Dr. Mortimer reports that Sir Charles's body showed no physical injury, his face was convulsed with terror, and there were footprints of a gigantic hound nearby. Chapter 14 resolves this: the 'hound' was a real dog made to look supernatural with phosphorus, and Stapleton deliberately used the family legend to frighten Sir Charles to death, so the terror came from fear rather than a wound and the footprints came from the hound he set on him. One nuance is that the toe-walking detail is not explained by the quoted line alone, but the resolution does answer who and what caused the terror and the hound prints, so it genuinely pays off the setup.

leads.quote: I find that before the terrible event occurred several people had seen a creature upon the moor which corresponds with this Baskerville demon

resolved.answer: The creature was most likely the huge, savage hound Stapleton bought in London and hid in the Grimpen Mire. He used it, made diabolical by artificial means, to frighten the weak-hearted Sir Charles.
resolved.quote: Here he kennelled it and waited his chance.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 2 Dr. Mortimer saw something he took for a large black calf at the head of Sir Charles's drive, and Sir Charles's horror at it hinted at a connection to the family's hound legend. The resolution identifies it as Stapleton's huge hound, kept hidden in the Grimpen Mire and used to terrify the weak-hearted baronet. The quoted line ('Here he kennelled it and waited his chance') is brief and concerns the hiding rather than the glimpse itself, but together with the stated identification it answers the question of what the creature was.

questions.question: What is the pressing matter that must be decided within twenty-four hours?
questions.quote: A most practical, pressing matter, which must be decided within twenty-four hours.

resolved.answer: The pressing matter is what Mortimer should do about Sir Henry Baskerville, who arrives at Waterloo in about an hour; Holmes asks for twenty-four hours.

resolved.payoff: In chapter 2 Holmes calls the matter 'most practical, pressing' and says it must be decided within twenty-four hours, but he does not say what it is. Chapter 3 names it: Mortimer wants advice on what to do with Sir Henry Baskerville, the heir, who is about to arrive at Waterloo Station. That urgency fits the twenty-four-hour deadline and supplies the missing content. The claim that Holmes asks for twenty-four hours is a small embellishment, but the core answer matches the setup.

questions.question: Whom was Sir Charles waiting for at the moor-gate the night before leaving for London, and what frightened him into running?
questions.quote: Then, again, whom was he waiting for that night, and why was he waiting for him in the yew alley rather than in his own house?

leads.quote: I know why he was at the gate at that hour. It was to meet a woman.

resolved.answer: He was waiting at the gate for Laura Lyons, whose appointment Stapleton made her break, and the hound frightened him.
resolved.quote: He then, by a specious argument, prevented her from going, and so had the chance for which he had waited.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 3 Holmes asks whom Sir Charles was waiting for at the moor-gate on the night before his London departure, and why he was so frightened that he ran from the house. Chapter 15 answers that Sir Charles was there to keep an appointment with Laura Lyons. Stapleton talked her out of going, 'by a specious argument', which gave him 'the chance for which he had waited' to set the hound on the unsuspecting baronet, and the hound is what drove Sir Charles to run to his death. The quoted line itself covers only the broken appointment and Stapleton's opportunity, not the hound by name, but it fits the setup's hints of a deliberate meeting, a long wait, and a terror that came across the moor.

questions.question: Was any crime actually committed, and if so by whom and how?
questions.quote: The one is whether any crime has been committed at all; the second is, what is the crime and how was it committed?

Chapter 15 answers both: Stapleton's 'ingenious mind' devised a way to kill Sir Charles, namely using a hound made to look supernatural, so a murder was committed by a living man by means of the 'devil's agent' of flesh and blood. The resolving quote is a partial lead-in to the method rather than the full explanation, but in context it introduces the hound-based murder plot and answers who and how.
