resolved.answer: Stapleton's wife sent the warning letter by cutting out words and addressing it in a disguised hand. Stapleton, disguised in a beard, had followed Dr. Mortimer to the Northumberland Hotel, which is how the hotel became known.
resolved.quote: disguised in a beard, followed Dr. Mortimer to Baker Street and afterwards to the station and to the Northumberland Hotel ... she adopted the expedient of cutting out the words which would form the message
resolved.payoff: The setup stresses that no one could have known about the Northumberland Hotel, since the choice was made only after Sir Henry met Dr. Mortimer, and that someone was 'very deeply interested in your movements.' It also shows a letter with printed, pasted words and a rough, printed address, posted at Charing Cross. The resolution answers both parts: Stapleton, disguised in a beard, tailed Mortimer from Baker Street to the station and then to the hotel, and his wife made the anonymous message by cutting out words, which explains the pasted-word construction and disguised address.

questions.question: Why was one of Sir Henry's new boots stolen?
questions.quote: It seems a singularly useless thing to steal

resolved.answer: The boot was taken to give the hound the scent; it was found in the mire.
resolved.quote: He retained it in his hand after using it to set the hound upon the track.
resolved.payoff: Holmes calls the theft 'singularly useless' and expects the boot to turn up, which hints that it was taken for a purpose other than its value. Chapter 14 supplies that purpose: the boot was taken to give the hound Sir Henry's scent, and its owner 'retained it in his hand after using it to set the hound upon the track.' The resolving quote supports the scent motive and the 'found in the mire' detail, though the quote alone doesn't spell out why a boot lost before it was worn would serve for scent.

questions.question: Could someone profit from Sir Henry's death, such as James Desmond or Barrymore, given the huge estate?
questions.quote: It is a stake for which a man might well play a desperate game.

resolved.answer: Yes. Stapleton stood to gain, since only two lives separated him from the valuable estate. James Desmond was cleared earlier as an amiable man, and Barrymore was not the beneficiary.
resolved.quote: The fellow had evidently made inquiry and found that only two lives intervened between him and a valuable estate.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 5 Holmes remarks that the near-million estate is 'a stake for which a man might well play a desperate game' and probes who would inherit, naming James Desmond (saintly, refused a settlement) as the apparent heir. Chapter 15 answers that someone did stand to profit: Stapleton, the hidden Baskerville heir, had learned that only two lives (Sir Charles and Sir Henry) stood between him and the estate, which explains his desperate scheme. The resolution also fits the setup's hints that Desmond was no real suspect, though Barrymore was dismissed on grounds the quoted line doesn't itself state.

questions.question: Who is the woman sobbing in the night at Baskerville Hall, and why?
questions.quote: It was the sob of a woman, the muffled, strangling gasp of one who is torn by an uncontrollable sorrow.

leads.text: Mrs. Barrymore, whose eyes are swollen and red, appears to be the woman who wept in the night and her husband must know of it, though the cause of her sorrow is not given.
leads.quote: It was she, then, who wept in the night, and if she did so her husband must know it.

resolved.answer: Mrs. Barrymore sobbed because of her brother Selden, the starving convict on the moor.
resolved.quote: My unhappy brother is starving on the moor. We cannot let him perish at our very gates.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 6 Watson hears a woman's muffled, strangling sob at night, an unexplained sign of uncontrollable sorrow inside the house. In chapter 9 it is revealed to be Mrs. Barrymore, weeping over her brother Selden, the escaped convict starving on the moor, and her statement that he is starving and cannot be left to perish at their gates directly supplies both the identity of the sobber and the reason for her grief.

questions.question: Why do the Barrymores really want to leave Baskerville Hall?
questions.quote: I fear that we shall never again be easy in our minds at Baskerville Hall.

leads.text: Mrs. Barrymore's confession that she is to blame and that her husband acted for her sake suggests a hidden secret (sheltering her brother) behind their unease, though the quote does not explicitly link it to wanting to leave the Hall.
leads.quote: That is the whole truth, as I am an honest Christian woman and you will see that if there is blame in the matter it does not lie with my husband but with me, for whose sake he has done all that he has.

leads.text: The Barrymores had a hidden burden, sheltering Mrs. Barrymore's convict brother, which suggests their unease at the Hall was not only grief for Sir Charles.
leads.quote: Every day we hoped that he was gone, but as long as he was there we could not desert him.

resolved.answer: Barrymore says he is alarmed by the sinister goings-on: Sir Charles's death, the noises on the moor and the hidden stranger. He wants to be "quit of it all" and to see Sir Henry safely back in London.
resolved.quote: There's foul play somewhere, and there's black villainy brewing, to that I'll swear!
resolved.payoff: In chapter 6 Barrymore blames grief over Sir Charles and says he and his wife "shall never again be easy in our minds at Baskerville Hall". That vague unease suggests a deeper reason that he leaves unspoken. In chapter 10 he drops the pretence and says he is alarmed by Sir Charles's death, the noises on the moor and the hidden stranger. He declares there is "black villainy brewing" and wants Sir Henry safely back in London, so the real motive is fear of the sinister events, not just sorrow. The resolution doesn't mention the Selden secret, but it does answer the question the setup raised.

questions.question: Why did Beryl Stapleton urgently warn Watson to leave, and what danger does she know of?
questions.quote: “Go back and never set foot upon the moor again.”

resolved.answer: Beryl, Stapleton's wife, sent the warning, evidently knowing of her husband's murderous scheme.
resolved.quote: “And the warning—it must have come from her!”
resolved.payoff: In chapter 7 Beryl urgently told Watson to leave the moor and never return, but would not explain, and she broke off when her brother approached. That showed she feared a danger and was hiding it from Stapleton. Chapter 12's "the warning—it must have come from her!" traces the warnings to Beryl as Stapleton's wife, and the danger is his scheme against the Baskerville heir. The quote only partly answers the question, since it names her as the source and leaves her motive and the specific danger to the surrounding context. Even so, it settles why she warned and what she knew.

questions.question: Is Stapleton hiding something, given his probing about Holmes and his watchfulness over his sister?
questions.quote: He spoke unconcernedly, but his small light eyes glanced incessantly from the girl to me.

resolved.answer: Yes. Holmes says Stapleton had laid a plot, and that he was shocked when the wrong man died in it.
resolved.quote: How he pulled himself together in the face of what must have been a paralyzing shock when he found that the wrong man had fallen a victim to his plot.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 7 Stapleton's small light eyes darted 'incessantly from the girl to me' and he questioned what she had said to Watson, hinting he feared she was warning the newcomer off a scheme. Chapter 12's resolution confirms he was concealing a murderous plot against Sir Henry, which explains his watchfulness over Beryl and his probing, and his 'paralyzing shock' at the wrong man dying fits a man with a deadly secret at stake.

questions.question: What caused the eerie moaning sound on the moor?
questions.quote: A long, low moan, indescribably sad, swept over the moor.

resolved.answer: The cries were the voice of the hidden hound, which Stapleton could not hush.
resolved.quote: He could hide his hound, but he could not hush its voice, and hence came those cries which even in daylight were not pleasant to hear.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 7 the long, low moan that swept the moor was explained by Stapleton as the peasants' legend of the Hound calling for its prey, a supernatural gloss that hid its real source. Chapter 14 reveals the sound was the voice of a real hound that Stapleton kept hidden in the mire but could not silence. This directly answers what caused the eerie moaning.

questions.question: Whom or what was Barrymore watching for from the empty room's window at night, and what was the key Watson heard turning?
questions.quote: His profile was half turned towards me, and his face seemed to be rigid with expectation as he stared out into the blackness of the moor.

leads.text: Watson's guess that the candle was a signal awaiting an answer suggests Barrymore was signalling someone out on the moor, though the quote names no one and says nothing about the key.
leads.quote: “He must have been holding it as a signal,” said I. “Let us see if there is any answer.”

resolved.answer: Barrymore was watching for an answering light from his wife's brother, the escaped convict Selden, hiding on the moor. The window light was a signal that food was ready for him. The passage does not explain the key Watson heard turning.
resolved.quote: But every second night we made sure if he was still there by putting a light in the window, and if there was an answer my husband took out some bread and meat to him.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 8, Barrymore crouches at the empty room's window with a candle, rigid with expectation, staring into the moor's blackness, then groans and puts the light out when nothing comes. The resolving quote explains this: the candle was a signal, put in the window every second night, and if an answer came from the moor he took bread and meat out to the man hiding there, Mrs. Barrymore's brother Selden. This settles the main mystery of whom he was watching for and why. The key Watson heard turning is not explained by this passage, so that minor detail stays open, but the core question is answered.

questions.question: What is the plan of campaign Watson and Sir Henry made after Barrymore's night walk?
questions.quote: I have had a long talk with Sir Henry this morning, and we have made a plan of campaign founded upon my observations of last night.

resolved.answer: The plan was for Watson and Sir Henry to sit up at night in Sir Henry's rooms, listening for Barrymore's movements in the passage. They kept watch for two nights until they heard him.
resolved.quote: I sat up with Sir Henry in his rooms until nearly three o’clock in the morning, but no sound of any sort did we hear except the chiming clock upon the stairs.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 8 Watson says he and Sir Henry made a 'plan of campaign' founded on his observations of Barrymore's night walk (the stealthy steps, the candle at the window, the key turning in a lock), but he withholds the details. Chapter 9 reveals it: the two men sat up together in Sir Henry's rooms until nearly three in the morning, listening for Barrymore's movements, and heard only the chiming clock on the stairs. The quoted passage confirms the nightly watch, though it covers only the first fruitless vigil, so the proposed answer's claim of 'two nights until they heard him' goes beyond what the quote shows.

questions.question: Why does Stapleton oppose a romance between Sir Henry and his sister?
questions.quote: Yet I am certain that he does not wish their intimacy to ripen into love

resolved.answer: Stapleton's supposed sister is really his wife, and he wanted her useful as a free woman.
resolved.quote: He took particular care that Sir Henry did not make love to her, as you have yourself observed.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 8, Watson notices that Stapleton looks disapproving whenever Sir Henry pays attention to Beryl and keeps them from being alone together, even though the match would seem advantageous. Chapter 12 explains this: the supposed sister is really Stapleton's wife, passed off as unmarried, so he cannot let Sir Henry's attentions become a real courtship. The resolving quote directly confirms that he took care to stop Sir Henry from making love to her, as Watson had observed. The proposal's wording that he wanted her 'useful as a free woman' is clumsy, but the core answer, that she is his wife and the romance must be prevented, fits the setup.

questions.question: Who is the tall, thin man on the tor, and is he a warder or something else?
questions.quote: There, outlined as black as an ebony statue on that shining background, I saw the figure of a man upon the tor.

resolved.answer: The man on the tor was Holmes.
resolved.quote: You saw me, perhaps, on the night of the convict hunt, when I was so imprudent as to allow the moon to rise behind me?
resolved.payoff: In chapter 9 Watson sees a tall, thin, motionless figure silhouetted on the tor against the moon, who vanishes when he turns to point him out, and he wonders whether it is the convict or a spirit of the moor. In chapter 12 Holmes admits he was that man, recalling that he let the moon rise behind him on the night of the convict hunt. This explains the silhouette and the moonlit backdrop, and shows he was a watcher, not a supernatural being or a warder.

questions.question: Why did Stapleton react so violently to the courtship, and is his apology sincere?
questions.quote: “I don’t say now that he isn’t a crazy man,” said Sir Henry; “I can’t forget the look in his eyes when he ran at me this morning, but I must allow that no man could make a more handsome apology than he has done.”

leads.text: Stapleton's own explanation is that fear of losing his sister made him lose control. Earlier Watson had noticed his disapproval of the courtship, and nothing yet settles whether the apology is sincere.
leads.quote: His sister is everything in his life, he says.

resolved.answer: Stapleton's outburst was jealousy, which broke through even though the courtship suited his own plan. His apology was not sincere: it was a pretence to keep Sir Henry coming to Merripit House.
resolved.quote: Stapleton himself seems to have been capable of jealousy, and when he saw the baronet paying court to the lady, even though it was part of his own plan, still he could not help interrupting with a passionate outburst

questions.question: What is the real source of the hound-like cry from the direction of Grimpen Mire?
questions.quote: It came with the wind through the silence of the night, a long, deep mutter, then a rising howl, and then the sad moan in which it died away.

resolved.answer: The hound-like cry came from the hound kept on the mire island.
resolved.quote: He could hide his hound, but he could not hush its voice, and hence came those cries which even in daylight were not pleasant to hear.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 9 the strange cry (a long mutter, rising howl, and moan) is dismissed as 'a sound they have on the moor' while Sir Henry instantly identifies it as the cry of a hound, hinting at a real animal behind the legend. Chapter 14 confirms this: Stapleton kept a real hound hidden on the mire island and could not silence its voice, so the cries heard on the moor, including at night, were the animal itself. The resolving quote directly answers the question of the cry's true source, though 'the hound kept on the mire island' is a slightly loose paraphrase of Stapleton's hidden hound in the Grimpen Mire.

questions.question: Is Laura Lyons the L. L. who arranged to meet Sir Charles at the gate, and what did she know of his death?
questions.quote: I expect if we could lay our hands upon that lady we should know more about Sir Charles’s death.

resolved.answer: Laura Lyons wrote the letter to Sir Charles, but Stapleton dictated it and then dissuaded her from keeping the appointment. She never dreamed of harm to Sir Charles, though she suspected Stapleton afterwards and stayed silent because he frightened her.
resolved.quote: He dictated it.

questions.question: Who is the hidden stranger in the stone huts, and is he the man on the tor and the London watcher?
questions.quote: A kind of gentleman he was, as far as he could see, but what he was doing he could not make out.

resolved.answer: The hidden man in the hut, and the figure on the tor, is Sherlock Holmes himself, living there with Cartwright's help. The man who dogged them in London was Stapleton, not Holmes.
resolved.quote: You saw me, perhaps, on the night of the convict hunt, when I was so imprudent as to allow the moon to rise behind me?

questions.question: Why is Holmes giving so little attention to the case, and will he come down to Dartmoor?
questions.quote: I am much mistaken if it does not bring him down.

resolved.answer: Holmes had secretly come to Dartmoor and was investigating on his own.
resolved.quote: it was my appreciation of the danger which you ran which led me to come down and examine the matter for myself.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 10 Watson notes that Holmes's notes from Baker Street are few and short, with hardly any reference to the Dartmoor mission, and he attributes this to the blackmailing case while predicting the L. L. clue will 'bring him down.' The chapter 12 resolution reveals that Holmes was not neglecting the case: he had secretly come to Dartmoor to examine the matter himself because he appreciated the danger to Sir Henry. This answers both parts of the question, since his apparent inattention was a cover and he did come down to Dartmoor.

questions.question: What private matter prevented Laura Lyons from keeping the appointment, and who helped her financially in the interval?
questions.quote: “No, I swear it to you on all I hold sacred. I never went. Something intervened to prevent my going.”

resolved.answer: Stapleton dissuaded her from keeping the appointment, saying it would hurt his self-respect for another man to find the money for her divorce.
resolved.quote: He told me that it would hurt his self-respect that any other man should find the money for such an object, and that though he was a poor man himself he would devote his last penny to removing the obstacles which divided us.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 11 Mrs. Lyons swore she never went to the garden meeting because 'something intervened', which she called a private matter, and the hint was that someone else was involved. Chapter 13 resolves this: Stapleton persuaded her not to keep the appointment, saying it would hurt his self-respect for another man to find the money for her divorce, and that he would give his last penny to remove the obstacles himself. This names Stapleton as the intervening influence and the one offering financial help in place of Sir Charles. The proposal does not state outright that he actually paid her in the interval, but the passage answers the central question.

questions.question: How did Selden know in the dark that the hound was on his trail, to be driven into such terror?
questions.quote: How came Selden, in the darkness, to know that the hound was on his trail?

resolved.answer: Selden saw the glowing hound bounding after him in the dark.
resolved.quote: No wonder the poor devil of a convict ran and screamed, even as our friend did, and as we ourselves might have done, when he saw such a creature bounding through the darkness of the moor upon his track.
resolved.payoff: Holmes asked how Selden, in darkness, could know the hound was on his trail and be driven to such terror that he screamed for help; Watson's earlier answer 'He heard him' was rejected as insufficient. The resolving passage supplies the answer: the hound was made to glow with phosphorus, so Selden saw a monstrous luminous creature bounding through the darkness after him, which explains both his knowledge of the pursuit and his paroxysm of terror.

questions.question: Why was the hound loose tonight, and how did Stapleton expect Sir Henry to be on the moor?
questions.quote: Stapleton would not let it go unless he had reason to think that Sir Henry would be there.

resolved.answer: Stapleton let the hound loose on the day he regarded as the end of his efforts, when Sir Henry would walk home across the moor.
resolved.quote: it was only on the supreme day, which he regarded as the end of all his efforts, that he dared do it.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 12 Watson reasons that Stapleton would not loose the hound unless he had reason to think Sir Henry would be on the moor, and Holmes admits the question may stay a mystery. Chapter 14 answers it: the hound was kept in check and released only on the 'supreme day' Stapleton saw as the culmination of his plan, when Sir Henry, after dining at Merripit House, would walk home alone across the moor. That confirms Watson's inference that the release was deliberate and tied to Sir Henry's expected presence, so the resolution fits the setup.

questions.question: What is Holmes's plan to prove the connection between Stapleton and the hound, and will Laura Lyons help?
questions.quote: I have great hopes of what Mrs. Laura Lyons may do for us when the position of affairs is made clear to her.

resolved.answer: Holmes's plan: feign departure to London, have Sir Henry walk home alone across the moor, and win Laura Lyons to testify against Stapleton, which she does.
resolved.quote: His plan of campaign was beginning to be evident.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 12 Holmes says he has no case yet, hopes Laura Lyons will help once the position is made clear to her, and has a separate plan of his own. Chapter 13 pays this off: Holmes shows Lyons that Stapleton used her and dictated the letter to Sir Charles, and she turns against him and gives the information Holmes wanted. Watson's remark that 'his plan of campaign was beginning to be evident' then introduces the second plan. Holmes and Watson will feign a departure for London while Sir Henry walks home alone across the moor as bait. The resolution slightly overstates Lyons's role as formal testimony, but it correctly answers both parts of the question.

questions.question: How is Stapleton related to the Baskervilles and what will the trap on the moor with Sir Henry walking alone achieve?
questions.quote: “This time you may do it with safety. If I had not every confidence in your nerve and courage I would not suggest it, but it is essential that you should do it.”

resolved.answer: Stapleton is Rodger Baskerville's son and so an heir; the trap caught him in the act.
resolved.quote: There seemed to be no alternative but to catch him red-handed, and to do so we had to use Sir Henry, alone and apparently unprotected, as a bait.
resolved.payoff: In chapter 13 Holmes insists Sir Henry walk home alone across the moor, saying 'this time you may do it with safety' while contradicting his earlier warnings, which hints that Sir Henry is deliberately being used as bait. Chapter 15 confirms this: Holmes says there was no alternative but to catch Stapleton red-handed, using Sir Henry alone and apparently unprotected as bait, and Stapleton is revealed as Rodger Baskerville's son and thus an heir. The resolution answers both parts of the question, the kinship and the purpose of the trap.

questions.question: How would Stapleton have claimed the Baskerville inheritance without exposing himself?
questions.quote: We cannot doubt from what we know of him that he would have found some way out of the difficulty.

resolved.answer: Holmes says Mrs. Stapleton heard her husband weigh three courses: claim the estate from South America without coming to England, use an elaborate disguise during a brief stay in London, or put an accomplice in as heir with the proofs and keep a share of the income. Holmes does not say which he would have chosen.
resolved.quote: He might claim the property from South America, establish his identity before the British authorities there and so obtain the fortune without ever coming to England at all
resolved.payoff: The question asks how Stapleton could claim the inheritance without exposing himself, and the setup is the same passage where Holmes says the problem is hard because it concerns future action. The resolution supplies the answer within it: Mrs. Stapleton heard him weigh three courses (claiming from South America without coming to England, a disguise during a short stay in London, or an accomplice installed as heir with a retained share of income). Holmes explicitly leaves the choice open, so the resolution correctly reports the options rather than a single decided method, which is all the text offers.

volumes.name: The Hound of the Baskervilles

arcs.name: The Baskerville Legend and Sir Henry's Arrival
arcs.summary:
At 221B Baker Street, Sherlock Holmes challenged Dr. Watson to deduce the character of a visitor, Dr. James Mortimer, from a walking stick left behind the night before. Watson judged Mortimer an elderly country doctor, but Holmes corrected him, inferring a young Charing Cross Hospital house-surgeon who owned a spaniel. Mortimer returned with his dog on the doorstep, proving Holmes largely right, though he was mistaken about the occasion of the gift, which was Mortimer's marriage. Mortimer said he faced a serious and extraordinary problem, and Holmes pressed him to state it.

Mortimer read aloud a 1742 family manuscript entrusted to him by Sir Charles Baskerville. It told how the wicked Hugo Baskerville abducted a yeoman's daughter and chased her across the moor with hounds, only to be killed by a gigantic black hound that had supposedly plagued the family ever since. Mortimer then read a Devon County Chronicle report of Sir Charles's recent death in the yew alley of Baskerville Hall, which the inquest ruled natural, with the heir, Henry Baskerville, then in America. Mortimer confided facts he had withheld from the inquest: Sir Charles's obsession with the legend, a black calf-like creature seen weeks earlier, and fresh footprints near the body that he declared were those of a gigantic hound. Questioned further by Holmes about the yew alley and the moor-gate, he admitted he half-believed the supernatural explanation, since three people had seen a spectral creature on the moor before Sir Charles died. Holmes told him to meet Sir Henry, who was farming in Canada and due at Waterloo, say nothing, and bring him to Baker Street the next morning. Holmes spent the day studying an Ordnance map of the moor and reasoned that Sir Charles had been running in terror, not walking on tiptoe, and had been waiting for someone at the moor-gate.

Next morning Mortimer brought Sir Henry Baskerville to Baker Street, where Sir Henry showed an anonymous letter of words pasted from the Times warning him to keep away from the moor. Holmes deduced the words came from a Times leader, that nail-scissors and gum were used, and that the address was probably written in a hotel. Sir Henry also reported a newly bought boot stolen from outside his hotel door. Hearing Mortimer's story, he resolved to go to Baskerville Hall regardless of danger. Holmes and Watson followed the two men through Regent Street and spotted a bearded man watching from a hansom cab, who escaped, though Holmes noted the cab number 2704. Holmes sent the messenger boy Cartwright to search the waste-paper of twenty-three Charing Cross hotels for the mutilated Times page.

At the Northumberland Hotel, Holmes found from the register that those watching Sir Henry were not lodging there. Sir Henry was furious over a second missing boot, an old black one, while the missing brown boot turned up under a cabinet. Holmes asked Mortimer about Barrymore, who had a black beard, and about Sir Charles's will, learning that the estate was close on a million, with seven hundred and forty thousand pounds left to Sir Henry and the entail passing to the Desmonds. Because a blackmail case kept him in London, Holmes asked Watson to accompany Sir Henry to Devonshire on Saturday's ten-thirty train from Paddington. Telegrams showed Barrymore was at the Hall and that Cartwright could not trace the Times sheet. The cabman John Clayton then revealed that his bearded fare had given the name Sherlock Holmes, which broke the third thread, and Holmes admitted he was uneasy about sending Watson.

arcs.name: Watson's Watch at Baskerville Hall
arcs.summary:
Holmes saw Watson, Sir Henry and Dr. Mortimer off from the station, instructing Watson to report facts only and to keep watch on those around Sir Henry, including the Barrymores, Stapleton and his sister, and Mr. Frankland. He warned Sir Henry never to go out alone or to walk the moor in the dark. In Devon the party saw soldiers hunting Selden, the Notting Hill murderer escaped from Princetown. Perkins drove them to Baskerville Hall, where Barrymore received them and said that he and his wife wished to leave. That night Watson lay awake and heard a woman sobbing somewhere in the house.

The next morning Barrymore denied that his wife had been crying, but Watson saw her red, swollen eyes and concluded he had lied. At Grimpen, Watson learned that the test telegram had been handed to Mrs. Barrymore rather than to Barrymore, so the test proved nothing. On the way back he met the naturalist Stapleton, who showed him the deadly Grimpen Mire, a pony dying in it, a strange moaning sound on the moor and the prehistoric stone huts. Stapleton's sister Beryl urged Watson to return to London, mistaking him for Sir Henry, and later retracted it as a whim born of fear of the family curse. In his first report to Holmes, dated October 13th, Watson described Sir Henry's growing attraction to Miss Stapleton, which her brother seemed to disapprove of, and the neighbour Frankland with his telescope. He also told how he had followed Barrymore at night and seen him staring out at the moor from an empty room's window with a candle.

In his second report Watson told how he and Sir Henry confirmed the window and kept watch. Sir Henry slipped off to meet Miss Stapleton on the moor, and Stapleton ran at them in a rage and led his sister away. He later apologised, and it was agreed that Sir Henry would court her only as a friend for three months, with the men to dine at Merripit House on Friday. On the second night's vigil they caught Barrymore signalling with a candle, and Mrs. Barrymore revealed that she was the sister of Selden, whom they were feeding on the moor. The two men chased Selden near the Cleft Tor after hearing a hound-like cry, and Watson glimpsed a tall, thin, unknown man standing on a tor. Next day Barrymore protested the hunting of Selden and promised that the convict would soon sail for South America, and Sir Henry agreed not to tell the police. Barrymore also revealed that Sir Charles had received a letter from Coombe Tracey signed L. L., asking him to be at the gate at ten, and that his wife had found its charred remains. Dr. Mortimer told Watson of Laura Lyons, Frankland's estranged daughter in Coombe Tracey, whose initials were L. L. Barrymore added that Selden knew of a gentleman-like stranger living in the stone huts and fed by a lad.

Watson drove to Coombe Tracey and questioned Mrs. Laura Lyons, who admitted writing the letter asking Sir Charles to meet her at the gate at ten but swore she never went, citing a private matter and her need for money for a divorce. Watson found her story coherent but felt something was held back. On the way back Frankland gloated over his legal victories and revealed that he had seen, through his telescope, a boy carrying food to a hidden person on the moor. Watson followed the boy's path to a circle of stone huts near Black Tor and found a clearly inhabited hut, with a note reading 'Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.' Waiting in the dusk with his revolver cocked, he heard footsteps and was greeted by a well-known voice.

arcs.name: The Hound's Undoing
arcs.summary:
In the stone hut near Black Tor, Watson discovered that the hidden stranger on the moor was Sherlock Holmes, who had been lodging secretly nearby with the boy Cartwright and had read all of Watson's reports. Holmes revealed that Stapleton was a former schoolmaster, that his supposed sister Beryl was in fact his wife, and that he was plotting murder. A terrible scream and the rumble of a hound drew the two across the moor, where they found a body in Sir Henry's ruddy tweed suit. It proved to be the convict Selden, wearing old clothes Barrymore had passed on to him. Stapleton arrived, visibly shaken to find the wrong man dead, and Holmes pretended he was returning to London while privately explaining that they lacked proof. Holmes then walked with Watson to Baskerville Hall, ordering him to say nothing of the hound to Sir Henry.

At the Hall, Holmes asked Sir Henry to obey him blindly and explained little. Studying the family portraits, he saw that the portrait of the wicked Hugo bore a striking resemblance to Stapleton, and concluded that Stapleton was a Baskerville with designs on the succession. Next morning he arranged a ruse: he and Watson would feign leaving for London while Sir Henry walked home alone across the moor from Merripit House after dining with the Stapletons. At Coombe Tracey Holmes wired Lestrade, who was coming with an unsigned warrant, and visited Laura Lyons. He showed her proof that Stapleton was married to Beryl, and in fury she confessed that Stapleton had dictated the letter to Sir Charles, then dissuaded her from keeping the appointment and made her stay silent. Holmes met Lestrade at the station and promised him a night on Dartmoor.

That night Holmes, Watson and Lestrade hid near Merripit House, where Watson saw Stapleton leave the dining-room and briefly visit an out-house while Sir Henry dined. Fog rolled in from Grimpen Mire, but Sir Henry emerged to walk home and was pursued by a huge black hound daubed with phosphorus. It knocked him down, and Holmes and Watson shot it dead. Searching Merripit House, they found Beryl Stapleton bound and whipped in the museum room; she told them Stapleton's refuge was an old tin mine on an island in the mire. Stapleton was never found. Next morning they followed her marked path into the mire, recovered Sir Henry's missing boot, and concluded that Stapleton had drowned in the bog. On the island they found the hound's kennel, the skeleton of a spaniel and the luminous paste, and Holmes explained how the device had been used to terrify Sir Charles and Selden.

At the end of November in Baker Street, Holmes, free of two other cases, recounted the whole affair to Watson. Stapleton, he explained, was the son of Rodger Baskerville, who had fled to England as Vandeleur, run a failing school in Yorkshire, and then moved to Devon to claim the estate. Holmes detailed how the phosphorus-daubed hound had killed Sir Charles, how Laura Lyons and Beryl had been used and manipulated, and how the boot, the warning letter and the shadowing in London fit together. He described his own secret stay on the moor with Cartwright and the bait plan that ended in Stapleton's destruction. With Sir Henry and Mortimer about to take a long voyage, Holmes closed by inviting Watson to the opera and dinner.

key_events.event: Dr. Mortimer consulted Sherlock Holmes about the mysterious death of Sir Charles Baskerville, revealing the family's hound legend and the gigantic hound footprints he had withheld from the inquest.

Sir Henry Baskerville, the heir, arrived in London and, after receiving an anonymous warning letter and losing a boot, was shadowed by a bearded man in a cab, leading Holmes to take up the case and send Watson to Baskerville Hall with him.

Watson discovered that Barrymore had been signaling with a candle in the window to the escaped convict Selden, who was Mrs. Barrymore's younger brother, and the Barrymores had been secretly feeding him on the moor.
Watson learned that Laura Lyons had written the letter asking Sir Charles to meet her at the gate on the night he died, and she named Stapleton as one of the people who had helped her.

Holmes revealed that he had been secretly on the moor all along and exposed Stapleton as a plotting murderer who had passed off his wife as his sister, and he confronted Stapleton after the hound was set on Selden.
Holmes and Watson, with Lestrade's help, learned that Stapleton was a Baskerville, and Laura Lyons confessed that Stapleton had dictated the letter that lured Sir Charles to his death.

deaths.name: Selden
deaths.circumstances: Selden, the escaped convict from Princetown, fled across the moor in Sir Henry's old boots, shirt and cap, which Barrymore had passed on to help his escape. Holmes concludes that the Hound of the Baskervilles was laid on him from an article of Sir Henry's, probably the boot stolen at the hotel, and ran him down. His body is found on the page by Watson and Holmes among the rocks, where Stapleton is told he appears to have broken his neck in a fall.
quotes: It is clear enough that the hound has been laid on from some article of Sir Henry’s—the boot which was abstracted in the hotel, in all probability—and so ran this man down.
Boots, shirt, cap—it was all Sir Henry’s.
“It is Selden, the man who escaped from Princetown.”

deaths.name: The Hound of the Baskervilles
deaths.circumstances: Stapleton had daubed the hound with a luminous phosphorus paste and set it upon Sir Henry's track using Sir Henry's missing boot, after keeping it chained in the island tin mine and the out-house at Merripit. On the moor, as it sprang at Sir Henry, Holmes emptied five barrels of his revolver into its flank, and it rolled over and fell limp. Watson pressed his pistol to its head to finish it, but found it already dead; the death happens on the page.

volumes.overview:
Chapters 1 to 15 of The Hound of the Baskervilles follow the detective Sherlock Holmes and his companion Dr. Watson as they confront a mystery rooted in the Baskerville family legend of a gigantic spectral hound. The story opens in London's Baker Street, where Dr. James Mortimer brings the case of Sir Charles Baskerville's sudden death in the yew alley of Baskerville Hall, and the arrival of the heir, Sir Henry, from Canada. It then moves to the Devon moor, with its Grimpen Mire, stone huts, an escaped convict named Selden and a cast of neighbours, before returning to Baker Street for a final retrospection.

The central conflict is between Holmes and a concealed murderer who exploits the curse to kill the Baskerville heirs. Watson, sent to guard Sir Henry and report to Holmes, gathers clues about the Barrymores, Laura Lyons, Frankland and the Stapletons, only to discover that Holmes has secretly been on the moor all along. Holmes identifies Stapleton as a Baskerville claimant who has posed as a naturalist and passed off his wife Beryl as his sister. Holmes sets a trap with Sir Henry as bait, the phosphorus-daubed hound is shot, and Stapleton is presumed drowned in the mire. Holmes then explains how the whole plot fit together.

development.development: Introduced as a brilliant armchair reasoner who deduces Mortimer's character from a walking stick, Holmes stays in London at first and sends Watson to Devon. He is revealed to have been secretly on the moor, directing events and testing Watson through the reports. He then sets a bait plan for Stapleton, and afterwards explains the whole affair, showing that his apparent absence was a calculated strategy.

Watson begins by misjudging Mortimer's character from the stick, but he grows into an active investigator, reporting from Baskerville Hall, following Barrymore, questioning Laura Lyons and tracking the hidden man to the stone hut. He is startled to find Holmes there, yet he proves a loyal and brave partner, helping to shoot the hound and later hearing Holmes's retrospection.

Sir Henry arrives from Canada, receives a threatening letter and loses boots, yet he resolves to go to Baskerville Hall regardless of danger. At the Hall he falls for Miss Stapleton, helps watch Barrymore and agrees to shelter Selden's secret. He finally obeys Holmes blindly and walks across the moor as bait, surviving the hound's attack.

He first appears as a friendly naturalist who shows Watson the Grimpen Mire and the moor's features, and he seems to disapprove of Sir Henry's attentions to his supposed sister. Holmes exposes him as a former schoolmaster and a Baskerville with designs on the estate, whose sister is really his wife. He is traced as the man behind the hound and the letter to Sir Charles, and he apparently drowns in the mire after the plan fails.

Mortimer first appears as a young country doctor with a spaniel who brings Holmes the Baskerville manuscript and admits he half-believes in a supernatural hound. He escorts Sir Henry to London and Devon and supplies information, such as Laura Lyons's identity. In the end he is about to take a long voyage with Sir Henry.

Presented as Stapleton's sister, she urgently warns Watson to leave, mistaking him for Sir Henry, and then retracts it as a whim born of fear of the curse. Holmes reveals that she is really Stapleton's wife, and she is found bound and whipped in Merripit House. She then reveals his refuge in the mire.

Watson finds her in Coombe Tracey, Frankland's estranged daughter, and she admits writing to Sir Charles but swears she never went to the gate. Her story seems coherent but she holds something back. When Holmes shows her proof that Stapleton is married to Beryl, she confesses in fury that Stapleton dictated the letter and made her stay silent.
